name: Nihali (Kalto)
lead: Nihali (also called Kalto or Nahali) is a Critically Endangered language isolate spoken in the Buldhana district of Maharashtra and the adjoining East Nimar (Burhanpur) district of Madhya Pradesh along the Tapti River valley in central India.[1][2] Although it has absorbed heavy lexical borrowing from Korku (Austroasiatic), Dravidian, and Marathi/Hindi, roughly 25% to 35% of its core Swadesh vocabulary—including pronouns, anatomical terms, and basic verbs—has no established external cognates.[1][2]
history: Nihali speakers have lived for centuries in a symbiotic socioeconomic relationship with the neighboring Korku (North Munda) community in villages around Jamod in Jalgaon Jamod tehsil.[1][2] F. B. J. Kuiper (1962) and Norman Zide analyzed its multilayered lexicon, noting that Nihali speakers also used a specialized register as a secret argot.[1] K. S. Nagaraja published a comprehensive descriptive grammar and lexicon in 2014.[2]
phonology: Nihali has a five-vowel quality system (/i, e, a, o, u/) with length distinctions and a consonant inventory typical of central Indian linguistic area languages, including retroflex stops (/ʈ, ʈʰ, ɖ, ɖʰ/) and a retroflex flap /ɽ/.[2]
syntax: Nihali is strictly SOV. Case suffixes attach directly to noun phrases: accusative/dative -ke / -na, ergative/instrumental -ka / -ki, genitive -n, and locative -mi / -ṭi.[2]
